verses.zh: 先知哈巴谷的祷告，调用流离歌。
verses.en: This is a prayer of Habakkuk the prophet:[NOTE:1]
notes: The Hebrew text adds עַל שִׁגְיֹנוֹת (ʿal shigyonot, “upon [or, “according to”] shigyonot”). The meaning of this word is uncertain. It may refer to the literary genre of the prayer or to the musical style to be employed when it is sung. The NEB leaves the term untranslated; several other modern English versions transliterate the term into English, sometimes with explanatory notes (NASB, NRSV “according to Shigionoth”; NIV “On shigyonoth”).

verses.zh: 耶和华啊，我听见你的名声（或译：言语）就惧怕。耶和华啊，求你在这些年间复兴你的作为，在这些年间显明出来；在发怒的时候以怜悯为念。
verses.en: Lord, I have heard the report of what you did;[NOTE:1] I am awed,[NOTE:2] Lord, by what you accomplished.[NOTE:3] In our time[NOTE:4] repeat those deeds;[NOTE:5] in our time reveal them again.[NOTE:6] But when you cause turmoil, remember to show us mercy![NOTE:7]
notes: Heb “your report,” that is, “the report concerning you.”
Heb “I fear.” Some prefer to read, “I saw, Lord, what you accomplished” (cf. NEB).
Heb “your work.”
Heb “in the midst of years.” The meaning of the phrase, which occurs only here in the OT, is uncertain (cf. NIV “in our day”; NEB, NASB “in the midst of the years”).
Heb “revive it” (i.e., “your work”).

Heb “make known.” The implied object is “your deeds”; the pronoun “them,” referring to “deeds” in the previous line, was employed in the translation to avoid redundancy. The suffix on the form חַיֵּיהוּ (khayyehu, “revive it”) does double duty in the parallelism.
Heb “in turmoil remember [to show] compassion.”

verses.zh: 神从提幔而来；圣者从巴兰山临到。（细拉）他的荣光遮蔽诸天；颂赞充满大地。
verses.en: God comes[NOTE:1] from Teman,[NOTE:2] the Holy One[NOTE:3] from Mount Paran.[NOTE:4] Selah.[NOTE:5] His splendor has covered the skies,[NOTE:6] the earth is full of his glory.[NOTE:7]
notes: In vv. 3-15 there is a mixture of eleven prefixed verbal forms (without vav [ו] consecutive or with vav conjunctive), sixteen suffixed forms, and three prefixed forms with vav consecutive. All of the forms are best taken as indicating completed action from the speaker’s standpoint (all of the prefixed forms being regarded as preterites). The forms could be translated with the past tense, but this would be misleading, for this is not a mere recital of God’s deeds in Israel’s past history. Habakkuk here describes, in terms reminiscent of past theophanies, his prophetic vision of a future theophany (see v. 7, “I saw”). From the prophet’s visionary standpoint the theophany is “as good as done.” This translation uses the English present tense throughout these verses to avoid misunderstanding. A similar strategy is followed by the NEB; in contrast note the NIV and NRSV, which consistently use past tenses throughout the section, and the NASB, which employs present tenses in vv. 3-5 and mostly past tenses in vv. 6-15.
Teman was a city or region in southern Edom.
Or “Sovereign One.” The term קָדוֹשׁ (qadosh, “holy [one]”) here refers to God’s sovereignty. See v. 3b.
The precise location of Mount Paran is unknown, but like Teman it was located to the southeast of Israel. Habakkuk saw God marching from the direction of Sinai.
Selah. The meaning of this musical term (which also appears in vv. 9, 13, and in the Psalms as well) is unknown.
Or “heavens.”

Heb “praise.” This could mean that the earth responds in praise as God’s splendor is observed in the skies. However, the Hebrew term תְּהִלָּה (tehillah, “praise”) can stand by metonymy for what prompts it (i.e., fame, glory, deeds).

verses.zh: 他的辉煌如同日光；从他手里射出光线，在其中藏着他的能力。
verses.en: His brightness will be as lightning;[NOTE:1] a two-pronged lightning bolt flashing from his hand.[NOTE:2] This is the outward display of his power.[NOTE:3]
notes: Heb “[His] radiance is like light.” Some see a reference to sunlight, but the Hebrew word אוֹר (ʾor) here refers to lightning, as the context indicates (see vv. 4b, 9, 11). The word also refers to lightning in Job 36:32 and 37:3, 11, 15.tc The subject, נֹגָהּ (nogah, “brightness”), is masculine but the verb is feminine. The LXX and most English translations add “his” to the subject. The verb form in the MT, an imperfect form of the stative verb הָיָה (hayah, “to be”) should always be future tense, as here in the LXX, and in English translations in the Psalms. But here most English translations use past or present. The BHS editors suggest emending the verb תִּהְיֶה (tihyeh) to the preposition and suffix תַּחְתָּיו (takhtayv) to make “[his] brightness is as lightning beneath him.” While this gets rid of the grammatical problem using similar looking consonants, it is speculative.

Heb “two horns from his hand [belong] to him.” Sharp, pointed lightning bolts have a “horn-like” appearance. The weapon of “double lightning” appears often in Mesopotamian representations of gods. See Elizabeth Van Buren, Symbols of the Gods in Mesopotamian Art (AnOr), 70-73. The term קֶרֶן (qeren), here in the dual form, commonly means “horn” but can also be used metaphorically (HALOT 1145 s.v. 4).

Heb “and there [is] the covering of his strength”; or “and there is his strong covering.” The meaning of this line is unclear. The point may be that the lightning bolts are merely a covering, or outward display, of God’s raw power. In Job 36:32 one reads that God “covers his hands with light [or, “lightning”].”

verses.zh: 在他前面有瘟疫流行；在他脚下有热症发出。
verses.en: Plague will go[NOTE:1] before him;pestilence[NOTE:2] will march[NOTE:3] right behind him.[NOTE:4]
notes: Or “goes.” The imperfect form of a dynamic verbal root may be either present or future. Here it is translated in parallel to the future tense in v. 4.

Because of parallelism with the previous line, the meaning “pestilence” is favored for רֶשֶׁף (reshef) here, but usage elsewhere suggests a destructive bolt of fire may be in view. See BDB 958 s.v. sn There are mythological echoes here, for in Canaanite literature the god Resheph aids Baal in his battles. See J. Day, “New Light on the Mythological Background of the Allusion to Resheph in Habakkuk III 5, ” VT 29 (1979): 353-55.
Or “marches.” See note 1.
Heb “will go out at his feet.”

verses.zh: 他站立，量了大地（或译：使地震动），观看，赶散万民。永久的山崩裂；长存的岭塌陷；他的作为与古时一样。
verses.en: He took his battle position[NOTE:1] and shook[NOTE:2] the earth;with a mere look he frightened[NOTE:3] the nations.The ancient mountains disintegrated;[NOTE:4] the primeval hills were flattened.His are ancient roads.[NOTE:5]
notes: Heb “he stood” or “took a stand.” The verb forms change to perfects and preterites in this verse, signaling past time and therefore a shift in perspective. The section starting here, the memory of the past, functions to certify the character of the future.
This verb has been traditionally understood as “measure” (from מָדַד, madad), but the immediately following context (vv. 6b-7) favors the meaning “shake” from מוּד (mud; see HALOT 555 s.v.).
Heb “he looked and made [the] nations jump back [in fear].”
Or “crumbled,” “broke into pieces.”

Heb “ancient ways [or, “doings”] are his.” The meaning of this line is unclear. Traditionally it has been translated, “his ways are eternal.” However, in this context (see vv. 3, 7) it is more likely that the line speaks of the Lord taking the same route as in the days of Moses and Deborah (see Deut 33:2; Judg 5:4). See J. J. M. Roberts, Nahum, Habakkuk, and Zephaniah (OTL), 154.

verses.zh: 我见古珊的帐棚遭难，米甸的幔子战兢。
verses.en: I saw the tents of Cushan overwhelmed by trouble;[NOTE:1] the tent curtains of the land of Midian were[NOTE:2] shaking.[NOTE:3]
notes: Cushan was located in southern Transjordan.tn Heb “under trouble I saw the tents of Cushan.”
The prefixed verb form is understood as past habitual just as the imperfect functions in background clauses in narrative.

R. D. Patterson takes תַּחַת אֲוֶן (takhat ʾaven) in the first line as a place name, “Tahath-Aven.” (Nahum, Habakkuk, Zephaniah [WEC], 237.) In this case one may translate the verse as a tricolon: “I look at Tahath-Aven. The tents of Cushan are shaking, the tent curtains of the land of Midian.”

verses.zh: 耶和华啊，你乘在马上，坐在得胜的车上，岂是不喜悦江河、向江河发怒气、向洋海发愤恨吗？
verses.en: Was[NOTE:1] the Lord mad at the rivers?Were you angry with the rivers?Were you enraged at the sea?[NOTE:2] Such that[NOTE:3] you would climb into your horse-drawn chariots,[NOTE:4] your victorious chariots?[NOTE:5]
notes: The verb is a perfect form and the root is stative so it could be past or present. Most translations render it as past (e.g. NASB, NIV, ESV, KJV, NRSV), though HCSB renders it present tense.
The following context suggests these questions should be answered, “Yes.” The rivers and the sea, symbolizing here the hostile nations (v. 12), are objects of the Lord’s anger (vv. 10, 15).
Heb “so that.” Here כִּי (ki) is resultative. See the note on the phrase “make it” in 2:18.
Heb “you mount your horses.” As the next line makes clear, the Lord is pictured here as a charioteer, not a cavalryman. Note NRSV here, “when you drove your horses, // your chariots to victory.”
Or “chariots of deliverance.”

verses.zh: 你的弓全然显露，向众支派所起的誓都是可信的。（细拉）你以江河分开大地。
verses.en: Your bow is ready for action;[NOTE:1] you commission your arrows.[NOTE:2] Selah.You cause flash floods on the earth’s surface.[NOTE:3]
notes: Heb “[into] nakedness your bow is laid bare.”

Heb “sworn in are the arrow-shafts with a word.” The passive participle of שָׁבַע (shava’), “swear an oath,” also occurs in Ezek 21:23 ET (21:28 HT) referencing those who have sworn allegiance. Here the Lord’s arrows are personified and viewed as having received a commission which they have vowed to uphold. In Jer 47:6-7 the Lord’s sword is given such a charge. In the Ugaritic myths Baal’s weapons are formally assigned the task of killing the sea god Yam.

As the Lord comes in a thunderstorm the downpour causes streams to swell to river-like proportions and spread over the surface of the ground, causing flash floods.tn Heb “[with] rivers you split open the earth.” A literal rendering like “You split the earth with rivers” (so NIV, NRSV) suggests geological activity to the modern reader, but in the present context of a violent thunderstorm, the idea of streams swollen to torrents by downpours better fits the imagery.

verses.zh: 山岭见你，无不战惧；大水泛滥过去，深渊发声，汹涌翻腾（原文是向上举手）。
verses.en: When the mountains see you, they shake.The torrential downpour sweeps through.[NOTE:1] The great deep[NOTE:2] shouts out;it lifts its hands high.[NOTE:3]
notes: Heb “a heavy rain of waters passes by.” Perhaps the flash floods produced by the downpour are in view here.
The great deep, which is to be equated with the sea (vv. 8, 15), is a symbol of chaos and represents the Lord’s enemies.
Lifting the hands here suggests panic and is accompanied by a cry for mercy (see Ps 28:2; Lam 2:19). The forces of chaos cannot withstand the Lord’s power revealed in the storm.

verses.zh: 因你的箭射出发光，你的枪闪出光耀，日月都在本宫停住。
verses.en: The sun and moon stand still in their courses;[NOTE:1] the flash of your arrows drives them away,[NOTE:2] the bright light of your lightning-quick spear.[NOTE:3]
notes: Heb “in their lofty dwelling places.”
Or “at the light of your arrows they vanish.”
Heb “at the brightness of the lightning of your spear.”

verses.zh: 你发忿恨通行大地，发怒气责打列国，如同打粮。
verses.en: You furiously stomp on the earth;you angrily trample down the nations.

verses.zh: 你出来要拯救你的百姓，拯救你的受膏者，打破恶人家长的头，露出他的脚（原文是根基），直到颈项。（细拉）
verses.en: You march out to deliver your people,to deliver your special servant.[NOTE:1] You strike the leader of the wicked nation,[NOTE:2] laying him open from the lower body to the neck.[NOTE:3] Selah.
notes: Heb “anointed one.” In light of the parallelism with “your people” in the preceding line this could refer to Israel, but elsewhere the Lord’s anointed one is always an individual. The Davidic king is the more likely referent here.
Heb “you strike the head from the house of wickedness.”
Heb “laying bare [from] foundation to neck.”

verses.zh: 你用敌人的戈矛刺透他战士的头；他们来如旋风，要将我们分散。他们所喜爱的是暗中吞吃贫民。
verses.en: You pierce the heads of his warriors[NOTE:1] with a spear.[NOTE:2] They storm forward to scatter us;[NOTE:3] they shout with joy as if they were plundering the poor with no opposition.[NOTE:4]
notes: Some take “warriors” with the following line, in which case one should translate, “you pierce [his] head with a spear; his warriors storm forward to scatter us” (cf. NIV). The meaning of the Hebrew term פְּרָזוֹ (perazo), translated here “his warriors,” is uncertain.
Heb “his shafts.” Some emend to “your shafts.” The translation above assumes an emendation to מַטֶּה (matteh, “shaft, spear”), the vav-yod (ו-י) sequence being derived from an original he (ה).
Heb “me,” but the author speaks as a representative of God’s people.
Heb “their rejoicing is like devouring the poor in secret.”

verses.zh: 你乘马践踏红海，就是践踏汹涌的大水。
verses.en: But you trample on the sea with your horses,on the surging, raging waters.[NOTE:1]
notes: Heb “the foaming of the mighty [or “many”] waters.”

verses.zh: 我听见耶和华的声音，身体战兢，嘴唇发颤，骨中朽烂；我在所立之处战兢。我只可安静等候灾难之日临到，犯境之民上来。
verses.en: I listened and my stomach churned;[NOTE:1] the sound made my lips quiver.My frame went limp, as if my bones were decaying,[NOTE:2] and I shook as I tried to walk.[NOTE:3] I long[NOTE:4] for the day of distressto come upon[NOTE:5] the people who attack us.
notes: Heb “my insides trembled.”
Heb “decay entered my bones.”

Heb “beneath me I shook, which….” The Hebrew term אֲשֶׁר (’asher) appears to be a relative pronoun, but a relative pronoun does not fit here. The translation assumes a reading אֲשֻׁרָי (’ashuray, “my steps”) as well as an emendation of the preceding verb to a third plural form.

The translation assumes that אָנוּחַ (’anuakh) is from the otherwise unattested verb נָוָח (navakh, “sigh”; see HALOT 680 s.v. II נוח; so also NEB). Most take this verb as נוּחַ (nuakh, “to rest”) and translate, “I wait patiently” (cf. NIV).
Heb “to come up toward.”

verses.zh: 虽然无花果树不发旺，葡萄树不结果，橄榄树也不效力，田地不出粮食，圈中绝了羊，棚内也没有牛；
verses.en: When[NOTE:1] the fig tree does not bud,and there are no grapes on the vines;when the olive trees do not produce[NOTE:2] and the fields yield no crops;[NOTE:3] when the sheep disappear[NOTE:4] from the penand there are no cattle in the stalls—
notes: Or “though.”
Heb “the produce of the olive disappoints.”
Heb “food.”
Or “are cut off.”

verses.zh: 然而，我要因耶和华欢欣，因救我的　神喜乐。
verses.en: I will rejoice because of[NOTE:1] the Lord;I will be happy because of the God who delivers me!
notes: Or “in.”

verses.zh: 主耶和华是我的力量；他使我的脚快如母鹿的蹄，又使我稳行在高处。这歌交与伶长，用丝弦的乐器。
verses.en: The Sovereign Lord is my source of strength.[NOTE:1] He gives me the agility of a deer;[NOTE:2] he enables me to negotiate the rugged terrain.[NOTE:3] (This prayer is for the song leader. It is to be accompanied by stringed instruments.)[NOTE:4]
notes: Or perhaps, “is my wall,” that is, “my protector.”
Heb “he makes my feet like those of deer.”

Heb “he makes me walk on my high places.” sn Difficult times are coming, but Habakkuk is confident the Lord will sustain him. Habakkuk will be able to survive, just as the deer negotiates the difficult rugged terrain of the high places without injury.
Heb “For the leader, on my stringed instruments.”
